title: Invertibility on a generating class
statement:
Let $\mathcal C,\mathcal D$ be triangulated categories [def-weil-triangulated-category], let $\Phi,\Psi:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ be exact functors, and let $\alpha:\Phi\to\Psi$ be a natural transformation compatible with their specified shift isomorphisms: for every $X$ and $n\in\mathbf Z$,
$$c_{\Psi,n,X}\circ\alpha_{X[n]}=\alpha_X[n]\circ c_{\Phi,n,X},\qquad c_{F,n,X}:F(X[n])\xrightarrow{\sim}F(X)[n].$$
If $\alpha_X$ is an isomorphism for every $X$ in a class $\mathcal G$, it is an isomorphism on the thick subcategory generated by $\mathcal G$, meaning the smallest full subcategory containing $\mathcal G$ and zero and closed under isomorphisms, finite direct sums, shifts, distinguished cones and retracts. In particular, if that subcategory is $\mathcal C$, then $\alpha$ is a natural isomorphism.

This propagates invertibility only. Natural transformations are not determined by their values on a thick generating class. Explicitly, let $R=\mathbf F_2[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$, let $\partial(a+b\epsilon)=b$, and write $\operatorname{Perf}(R)\subset D(R)$ for the category of perfect complexes [def-pc-perfect-ring-complex]. The derivation $\partial$ defines a natural transformation $\eta:\mathrm{Id}\to[1]$ on $\operatorname{Perf}(R)$ with $\eta_R=0$ and with $\eta_P\ne0$ for $P=[R\xrightarrow{\epsilon}R]$ in degrees $0,1$: under $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(R)}(P,P[1])\cong R/(\epsilon)$ its value is $1$. The object $R$ thickly generates $\operatorname{Perf}(R)$, but the natural automorphisms $\mathrm{id}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ \eta&1\end{pmatrix}$ of $\mathrm{Id}\oplus[1]$ agree on $R$ and differ on $P$. Thus agreement on a thick generating class does not by itself establish equality of comparison maps.

proof.text: Put $\mathcal S=\{X:\alpha_X\text{ is invertible}\}$. It contains $\mathcal G$ by hypothesis and zero since both exact additive functors take zero to zero. If $u:X\xrightarrow{\sim}Y$, naturality gives $\alpha_Y=\Psi(u)\alpha_X\Phi(u)^{-1}$, so $\mathcal S$ is closed under isomorphisms.

source.place: Proof: the isomorphism locus, zero, and closure under isomorphisms

proof.text:
For a distinguished triangle $X\xrightarrow{u}Y\xrightarrow{v}Z\xrightarrow{w}X[1]$, exactness of the two functors gives distinguished image triangles. Naturality supplies the first two squares; the last square is the explicit identity
$$c_{\Psi,1,X}\Psi(w)\alpha_Z=c_{\Psi,1,X}\alpha_{X[1]}\Phi(w)=\alpha_X[1]c_{\Phi,1,X}\Phi(w).$$
Thus $(\alpha_X,\alpha_Y,\alpha_Z)$ is a morphism of distinguished triangles, including its connecting square. Apply [lem-sf-triangle-morphism-iso]: invertibility at any two vertices implies invertibility at the third, so $\mathcal S$ is closed under distinguished cones.

source.place: Proof, first sentence: two-out-of-three; Stacks Tag 014A, lemma-third-isomorphism-triangle

proof.text: The assumed equation writes $\alpha_{X[n]}=c_{\Psi,n,X}^{-1}\alpha_X[n]c_{\Phi,n,X}$. Shifting an inverse supplies an inverse of $\alpha_X[n]$, and shifting back by $-n$ reflects invertibility. Hence $X\in\mathcal S$ if and only if $X[n]\in\mathcal S$. This uses compatibility of $\alpha$, not merely exactness of the two functors.

source.place: Proof: shifts; correction of the missing natural-transformation compatibility hypothesis

proof.text:
By additivity and naturality for the two inclusions and projections, $\alpha_{X\oplus Y}$ is the diagonal matrix with entries $\alpha_X,\alpha_Y$, so $\mathcal S$ is closed under finite sums. More generally let $i:X\to Y$, $p:Y\to X$ satisfy $pi=1_X$, and let $\beta_Y=\alpha_Y^{-1}$. Set $\beta_X=\Phi(p)\beta_Y\Psi(i)$. Naturality gives
$$\beta_X\alpha_X=\Phi(p)\beta_Y\alpha_Y\Phi(i)=1,\qquad \alpha_X\beta_X=\Psi(p)\alpha_Y\beta_Y\Psi(i)=1.$$
Thus $\mathcal S$ is closed under retracts, including every direct summand.

source.place: Proof: additivity and direct summands, expanded to retracts

proof.text: The preceding steps show that $\mathcal S$ is one of the full subcategories in the defining intersection for the thick subcategory generated by $\mathcal G$, so that intersection is contained in $\mathcal S$. If it is all of $\mathcal C$, the component inverses form a natural transformation: multiplying $\Psi(f)\alpha_X=\alpha_Y\Phi(f)$ by inverses gives $\alpha_Y^{-1}\Psi(f)=\Phi(f)\alpha_X^{-1}$. This proves the invertibility assertion.

source.place: Proof, final sentence: the thick-subcategory conclusion

proof.text:
For the counterexample work with bounded complexes of finitely generated projective $R$-modules, as in [def-pc-perfect-ring-complex]. The formula $\partial(a+b\epsilon)=b$ is additive and obeys the Leibniz rule, since the $\epsilon$ coefficient in $r\partial(s)+\partial(r)s$ is $2bd=0$ for $r=a+b\epsilon$, $s=c+d\epsilon$. On each projective module $M$ choose a splitting $M\xrightarrow{i}F\xrightarrow{p}M$ with $pi=1$ into a free module, supplied by [def-weil-pbc-projective-module]. Apply $\partial$ coordinatewise on $F$ and put $
abla_M=p\partial i$. Then
$$
abla_M(rm)=\partial(r)m+r
abla_M(m).$$
No freeness of the projective module itself is assumed.

proof.text:
If $f:A\to B$ is a chain map, put $b^i=\nabla_B^if^i-f^i\nabla_A^i$. Again $b^i$ is $R$-linear, and expansion of $d_Bf=fd_A$ gives
$$a_Bf-f[1]a_A=bd_A-d_Bb.$$
The right side is the homotopy boundary for maps $A\to B[1]$. Consequently the homotopy classes $[a_A]$ form a natural transformation from the identity to the shift on bounded projective complexes modulo homotopy. Since equality modulo homotopy is used here, the argument applies to every homotopy class of chain maps.

proof.text:
Apply [lem-pc-ring-derived-map-representative] with the abelian category of $R$-modules. Every model is bounded, hence bounded above, with projective terms, and the target may be any complex, including a shift. Its bijection identifies all derived morphisms between these models with chain maps modulo homotopy. By [def-pc-perfect-ring-complex], for each perfect object $X$ choose a model $A_X$ and an isomorphism $t_X:Q(A_X)\xrightarrow{\sim}X$, and set
$$\eta_X=t_X[1]\circ Q(a_{A_X})\circ t_X^{-1}.$$
For $f:X\to Y$, represent $t_Y^{-1}ft_X$ by a chain map $g:A_X\to A_Y$ using the bijection. Step 8 gives $Q(a_{A_Y})Q(g)=Q(g)[1]Q(a_{A_X})$; conjugating this identity by $t_X,t_Y[1]$ gives $\eta_Yf=f[1]\eta_X$. For another model $B_X$ with isomorphism $u_X:Q(B_X)\xrightarrow{\sim}X$, represent $u_X^{-1}t_X$ by a chain map and apply the same identity: $t_X[1]Q(a_{A_X})t_X^{-1}=u_X[1]Q(a_{B_X})u_X^{-1}$. Thus the definition is independent of the model and gives the required natural transformation on all of $\operatorname{Perf}(R)$.

proof.text:
This is also the bimodule-extension construction in the unit's statement. Give $E=R\oplus R$ its usual left action and the right action $(x,y)r=(xr+y\partial(r),yr)$. Associativity of this action is exactly the Leibniz identity, and $0\to R\xrightarrow{x\mapsto(x,0)}E\xrightarrow{(x,y)\mapsto y}R\to0$ is an exact sequence of bimodules. For a projective $M$, the map
$$s_M(m)=(0,1)\otimes m-(1,0)\otimes\nabla_M(m)\in E\otimes_RM$$
is $R$-linear: the balancing identity $(0,1)\otimes rm=r(0,1)\otimes m+(1,0)\otimes\partial(r)m$ cancels the Leibniz term. It splits the quotient onto $M$. Explicitly, $(u,v)\mapsto(1,0)\otimes u+s_M(v)$ is an isomorphism $M\oplus M\to E\otimes_RM$, with balanced inverse $(x,y)\otimes m\mapsto(xm+y\nabla_M(m),ym)$. Both composites are the identity by the displayed balancing and Leibniz formulas, so tensor exactness is not being inferred without checking it. In these degreewise splittings, $E\otimes_RA$ has differential $\begin{pmatrix}d_A&-a_A\\0&d_A\end{pmatrix}$. Its connecting chain map is $-a_A=a_A$, since $R$ has characteristic two. Thus the explicitly constructed $\eta$ realizes the very bimodule extension specified in the blueprint.

proof.text:
Finally $R$ is a thick generator of $\operatorname{Perf}(R)$. A finitely generated projective $M$ is a retract of a finite free module: choose finitely many generators, form the surjection $R^N\to M$, and split it by the lifting property in [def-weil-pbc-projective-module]. For a bounded projective complex $A$, put $L=A_{\ge q+1}$, $B=A_{\ge q}$ and $M=A^q[-q]$, using stupid tails. Graded-module splitting writes $B=L\oplus M$ and $d_B=\begin{pmatrix}d_L&t\\0&d_M\end{pmatrix}$ with $d_Lt+td_M=0$. For the inclusion $i:L\to B$, write $C(i)^r=L^r\oplus M^r\oplus L^{r+1}$; its differential is
$$d_C(x,m,z)=(d_Lx+tm+z,d_Mm,-d_Lz).$$
The projection $\pi(x,m,z)=m$ and the map $s(m)=(0,m,-tm)$ are chain maps with $\pi s=1$. The degree-minus-one map $H(x,m,z)=(0,0,x)$ satisfies $d_CH+Hd_C=(x,0,z+tm)=1-s\pi$, so $C(i)$ is homotopy equivalent to $M$. Hence the cone triangle of $i$ identifies with a distinguished triangle $L\to B\to M\to L[1]$; cone triangles and their images in the derived category are distinguished by [lem-pur-homotopy-category-triangulated]. Starting with the zero tail above the largest nonzero degree and descending finitely many times shows that $A$ belongs to the thick closure of its terms. Every perfect object has this model by [def-pc-perfect-ring-complex], so the closure of $R$ within $\operatorname{Perf}(R)$ is the whole category.

source.place: Counterexample paragraph: justification that the specified object R is a thick generator

proof.text: For every perfect $A$ let $T_A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ \eta_A&1\end{pmatrix}$ on $A\oplus A[1]$. Naturality of $\eta$ makes $T$ natural. Matrix multiplication shows that $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-\eta_A&1\end{pmatrix}$ is a two-sided inverse, so $T$ and the identity are natural automorphisms of $\mathrm{Id}\oplus[1]$. They agree at $R$ because $\eta_R=0$, and differ at $P$ because projecting their difference to the lower-left block gives $\eta_P\ne0$. This supplies the promised non-determination counterexample; it makes no assertion that equality of comparison maps follows from values on generators.

source.place: Counterexample paragraph: the displayed two natural automorphisms
